quick: Topical/oromucosal: apply to affected area up to 3-4 times daily (product-specific)
Avoid eating until oral/throat numbness resolves
Topical use; minimal systemic absorption, use if needed
No specific interaction with topical use
summary: Benzocaine is an ester-type local anesthetic used topically on skin and mucous membranes and in oral/throat products for short-term pain relief. Its principal serious risk is methemoglobinemia, which can occur even with appropriate use and especially in infants; for this reason oral benzocaine products are not recommended in children under 2 years. Systemic absorption from intact skin is low.
indications: Temporary relief of pain from minor mouth and throat irritation, canker sores, teething (limited), and oral procedures
Topical anesthesia of accessible mucous membranes prior to minor procedures
Temporary relief of pain and itching from minor skin conditions, sunburn, insect bites and minor burns
Local anesthesia for anorectal disorders (hemorrhoid products)

dosage.d: Apply gel/spray/lozenge to affected area up to 3-4 times daily as needed
dosage.n: Do not exceed product label; not for children <2 yr (oral)

dosage.d: Apply thin layer to affected area not more than 3-4 times daily
Apply to mucosa using lowest effective amount (e.g., spray <=1-2 seconds)
dosage.n: Limit spray duration to minimize methemoglobinemia risk

dosage.d: Apply to affected anorectal area up to 6 times daily per product

admin: For external/mucosal use only; apply the smallest effective amount
Limit spray applications to short bursts to reduce methemoglobinemia risk
Do not apply to large areas or broken/inflamed skin where absorption increases
Avoid eating or drinking until oral/throat numbness has resolved to prevent aspiration/biting injury
Avoid use of oral benzocaine in infants and children under 2 years
moa: Benzocaine is an ester local anesthetic that reversibly binds voltage-gated sodium channels in neuronal membranes, blocking sodium influx and preventing initiation and conduction of nerve impulses. This produces localized loss of sensation at the site of application.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to benzocaine or other ester-type local anesthetics (e.g., procaine, PABA)
Oral benzocaine products in children under 2 years (methemoglobinemia risk)
relative: Pre-existing or congenital methemoglobinemia, G6PD deficiency
Significant cardiac or respiratory disease (reduced tolerance to methemoglobinemia)
monitor: Application to large or denuded areas

preg: Topical/local use results in minimal systemic absorption; benzocaine may be used during pregnancy when needed. Avoid excessive application or use over large areas.
lact: With topical use, systemic exposure is minimal and benzocaine is generally considered compatible with breastfeeding; avoid application to the nipple just before nursing.
renal: No specific dose adjustment; systemic absorption from topical/mucosal use is minimal.
hepatic: No specific dose adjustment; benzocaine is metabolized by plasma esterases with minimal systemic exposure from topical use.

moderate: Other agents that induce methemoglobinemia (nitrates/nitrites, dapsone, sulfonamides, prilocaine, chloroquine) - additive risk
minor: Sulfonamide antibiotics - PABA (a benzocaine metabolite) may theoretically antagonize sulfonamide activity
interactions.food: Avoid food/drink until oral numbness resolves; otherwise no significant food interaction.
interactions.alcohol: No clinically significant interaction with topical use.
interactions.diagnostics: Can elevate measured methemoglobin; pulse oximetry may read falsely in methemoglobinemia.

common: Local burning or stinging on application
Transient numbness beyond the target area
emergency: Methemoglobinemia (cyanosis, gray/blue skin, shortness of breath, fatigue, headache, tachycardia)

monitoring: Signs of methemoglobinemia (bluish skin/lips, breathlessness, headache, light-headedness), especially in infants and after mucosal use
Local tissue tolerance with repeated use
Adequacy of swallowing/airway reflexes after oropharyngeal application
counsel: Use only as directed and use the smallest amount needed
Do NOT use oral benzocaine products in children under 2 years
Seek emergency care if skin, lips or nail beds turn gray or blue, or if you become short of breath, light-headed or unusually tired - these can be signs of a serious blood problem (methemoglobinemia)
Do not eat or drink until mouth/throat numbness wears off
Stop and consult a doctor if symptoms persist beyond a few days or worsen
pk: Rapid; topical anesthesia within ~30 seconds to a few minutes
Short; rapidly hydrolyzed by plasma cholinesterase
Store at room temperature; keep tightly closed and away from heat/flame (some sprays flammable)
pearls: FDA WARNING: Benzocaine can cause methemoglobinemia, sometimes with a single application; oral OTC products should NOT be used in children under 2 years
Treat significant methemoglobinemia with intravenous methylene blue (avoid in G6PD deficiency)
Ester anesthetic - cross-reactivity with PABA/procaine; ask about prior local anesthetic allergy
Very short duration of action; for prolonged anesthesia an amide agent is usually preferred
missed: Benzocaine is used as needed for symptom relief, not on a fixed dosing schedule, so there is no missed-dose concern. Reapply only when symptoms return and do not exceed the labeled frequency.
overdose: Excessive application can cause systemic toxicity and methemoglobinemia. For methemoglobinemia, give oxygen and intravenous methylene blue 1-2 mg/kg (contraindicated in G6PD deficiency); provide supportive care and monitor oxygenation. CNS or cardiovascular toxicity is managed symptomatically.
